1 John
furst jon
proper noun (a book of Scripture)
The first epistle of the apostle John, a pastoral letter written that believers might know they have eternal life and walk in light, love, and truth.

See also: 1 John

📖 Biblical Definition

First John is the first of the three epistles of the apostle John, a pastoral letter written to assure true believers and to guard them against the early errors that denied the incarnation. John opens with the witness of an eyewitness to the Word of life—“which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes… and our hands have handled”—grounding the faith in the real, bodily coming of the Son of God against the Gnostic and proto-docetic teachers who denied that Christ had come in the flesh. The epistle weaves together great themes: God is light, and the believer walks in the light, confessing sin and cleansed by the blood of Christ, our advocate with the Father; God is love, and he that loveth not knoweth not God; and the believer is called to love the brethren in deed and truth. John gives a series of tests by which a soul may discern whether its profession is true—obedience to the commandments, love of the brethren, and confession that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh—and states his purpose plainly: “These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life.” The dictionary holds First John to be the great epistle of Christian assurance, teaching that the believer may have real and settled knowledge of his salvation, grounded in the finished work of Christ and confirmed by the marks of true faith. It marks the book against two errors: the perfectionism that twists “he that is born of God sinneth not” into sinlessness in this life, when John also says that if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves; and the cheap assurance that claims to know God while walking in darkness and hating the brethren, which John flatly denies.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The apostle John's first epistle, grounding the faith in the eyewitnessed incarnation against early error, and teaching the tests of true faith; the great epistle of Christian assurance (1 John 5:13)—“that ye may know that ye have eternal life.”

expand to see more

1 JOHN, proper noun. The first epistle of the apostle John, a pastoral letter of assurance and truth.

It grounds the faith in the eyewitnessed, bodily coming of the Word of life (1 John 1:1).

Great themes: God is light, God is love, and the call to love the brethren (1 John 4:8).

It gives tests of true faith: obedience, brotherly love, and confessing Christ in the flesh.

Its purpose: “that ye may know that ye have eternal life” (1 John 5:13).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Jo 1:1 — "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life;"

1 Jo 4:8 — "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love."

1 Jo 5:13 — "These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God."

1 Jo 2:1 — "My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Perfectionism twists “born of God sinneth not” into sinlessness in this life, while cheap assurance claims to know God while walking in darkness; the liberal reduces “God is love” to sentiment severed from truth and holiness.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors mishandle First John's teaching on sin and assurance. Perfectionism seizes on “whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin” to claim a sinless state in this life, ignoring that the same epistle says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” John teaches that the believer does not practise sin as the settled course of his life, not that he is sinless. The opposite error is a cheap assurance that professes to know God while walking in darkness and hating the brethren; John denies it outright: “he that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now.”

The liberal corruption fastens on “God is love” and severs it from the truth and holiness that surround it, making love a sentiment that asks nothing of doctrine or obedience and affirms all things. But John defines the love of God as keeping His commandments, and grounds it in the propitiation of the cross—“herein is love… that he sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.” The dictionary holds First John whole: God is love and God is light; the believer may know he has eternal life; and that knowledge is confirmed, not contradicted, by obedience, brotherly love, and the confession that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The first of John's three epistles; its keynote verbs are “we know” (Greek oidamen) and “abide” (meno), marking assurance and communion with God.

expand to see more

Oidamen, Greek, “we know,” the recurring note of assurance in the epistle.

Meno, Greek, to abide or remain, of the believer's communion with God.

Koinonia, Greek, fellowship, with the Father and with one another.

Hilasmos, Greek, propitiation, the ground of love and forgiveness (1 John 2:2).

Written against early deniers of Christ's coming in the flesh.

Usage

"The pastor preached First John to give the doubting believer a settled assurance grounded in Christ."

"He answered perfectionism from the epistle's own “if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.”"

"She tested her profession by John's marks: obedience, love of the brethren, and confessing Christ in the flesh."
